cover.headline: India's eyewear category-builder: a better business every quarter, but the price already runs ahead of it
cover.lead: Lenskart designs, makes and sells glasses through 3,459 stores (2,725 in India) and an app, and owns Owndays (Japan) and Meller (Spain). It listed on 10-Nov-2025 at ₹402; the stock has risen 70% since. FY26 revenue grew 32.5% to ₹8,814 cr and EBITDA margin reached 19.9% (13.3% after rent in Q1FY27, against a ~25% long-term aim). We forecast EPS of ₹5.05 / ₹6.94 / ₹9.29 for FY27-29E, in the middle of the street. The street values Lenskart on **EV/EBITDA 1.5-2 years forward** (48-58x EBITDA after rent). The house rule (its own forward EV/EBITDA median since listing, 30.6x, adjusted by the retail peers' −11.6% move over the same ten months) gives **27x Sep-28E EBITDA of ₹3,540 cr = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with SELL.** That is ≈41.2x after-rent EBITDA on the street's basis. Cross-checks: P/E ₹592, DCF ₹402. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: The business is creating its own market, and it shows in the numbers
arguments.p: India revenue +30.7% in Q1FY27 with SSSG 18.3%, 63 lakh eye tests (+43%, half first-ever) and 116 net new stores; ~6,100 Indian pin codes still have no Lenskart store. Product margin crossed 70% as frames and lenses moved in-house. We model India +{{as.segments.0.growth.0|pct0}} / +{{as.segments.0.growth.1|pct0}} / +{{as.segments.0.growth.2|pct0}} on ~560 openings a year.

International (41% of revenue) went from a 3.6% margin after rent in FY25 to 7.0% in FY26 and 10.6% in Q1FY27, on same-store growth (+38%, ~29% in constant currency) with only 16 new stores. Meller is tracking towards ~US$70 mn. We take 21.0% before rent and ESOP in FY27E (Q1 is the sunglasses season).

Reported EBITDA (21.7% in Q1FY27) excludes rent under Ind AS 116; after rent the margin is 13.3%. On our numbers after-rent EBITDA rises from ~₹971 cr in FY26 to ₹2,533 cr in FY29E (~15.1% of revenue). Operating leverage is real, but SSSG is cooling (24% to 18% in two quarters) and openings move to smaller towns.

arguments.h: Valuation: the street pays for the next decade today
arguments.p: At ₹685.05 the stock trades at 33.4x Sep-28E EBITDA before rent and 98.7x FY28E EPS, above its 30.6x forward median since listing, while retail peers trade ~12% below their own medians over the same months. The street's median target (₹707, 12 post-results notes) needs 48-58x after-rent EBITDA. Pre-IPO funds (SoftBank, ADIA, Alpha Wave) have been selling into strength since May.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): India SSSG after 18.3% in Q1, International margin after the sunglasses season, store additions against the ~600 plan.
Further block sales by pre-IPO holders (SoftBank 7.3%, ADIA, PI Opportunities Fund, Macritchie, Steadview): supply on rallies.
Hyderabad plant (~18 months from May-2026): capex peak in FY27, then product-margin gains.
Acquisitions funded from the ₹683 cr IPO allocation and the ₹4,104 cr net cash.
Smart glasses (B by Lenskart): 80,000+ sign-ups by Aug-2026; no revenue in our model.

sections.title: An eye-test-to-delivery machine: it makes its own glasses and sells them through 3,459 stores and an app

blocks.p: Omnichannel eyewear company that designs, makes and sells prescription glasses, sunglasses, contact lenses and accessories. Owns the chain from frame and lens manufacturing (Bhiwadi, Rajasthan; Hyderabad plant under construction; 50% Thailand frame JV) and a central supply chain to 3,459 stores (Jun-2026: 2,725 India, 734 International), an app and website, home eye tests and remote optometry. Brands: Lenskart, John Jacobs, Vincent Chase, Owndays (Japan, acquired 2022), Meller (Spain, acquired FY26), Hustlr. International = Japan, Singapore and South-East Asia, the Middle East, Spain (Meller) and others (14 international markets, Q4FY26 letter). In FY26 revenue was ₹8,814 cr: India ₹5,260 cr (59%) and International ₹3,606 cr (41%). FY26: 23.8 mn eye tests, ~29 mn India eyewear units, 8.8 mn Lenskart Gold members, 20,000+ employees; ~50% of India revenue digitally influenced (55% in Q1FY27).

blocks.callout: **How it makes money:** Lenskart earns a ~70% product margin (revenue less the cost of frames and lenses) because it designs, makes and sells its own glasses: the Bhiwadi plant makes frames and lenses for India and much of International, and a central lab ships made-to-order glasses next day in 78 cities. From that margin it pays staff (optometrists in every store), rent and marketing. Every eye test is the top of the funnel: 23.8 mn in FY26, about half of them first-ever tests in India. Gold, a paid membership (8.8 mn members, ₹200 cr of fees in FY26), keeps customers coming back.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** about 40% of revenue and most of the goodwill came through acquisitions, and the FY25-26 franchise buy-back changed the cost structure (commissions down, staff and rent up). The clean, like-for-like history is short: the company itself presents "proforma" numbers to bridge it. Lenskart has shown it can integrate (Owndays' margin is up, Meller has doubled), but acquisitions remain part of the plan.

sections.title: India needs 78 cr pairs of eyes corrected and only 35% of them wear glasses: a market that grows by being created

blocks.p: The company's own build of the Indian market (AR FY26, using Redseer and government data): 145 cr people, 53% needing vision correction (77.7 cr), only 35% of them actually using correction (27.4 cr), 0.88 pairs a year each: 24.2 cr pairs at ~₹2,370 = ₹573 bn of prescription eyewear in FY25, ₹788 bn including contact lenses and sunglasses (₹894 bn estimated for FY26). By FY30 it projects 62% needing correction, 41% penetration, ₹1,478 bn. India imported 44 cr ophthalmic lenses in FY25 (~22 cr pairs), up 11% a year in volume since FY19 (DGCIS).

Most of the market is still unorganised: neighbourhood opticians who buy frames and lenses from wholesalers and test eyes by hand. Lenskart had a 4-6% share of Indian prescription eyewear in FY25 (RHP via ICICI Direct, 30-Oct-2025). Abroad, its markets (South-East Asia, Japan, Middle East) were a ₹1,716 bn eyewear market in FY26, growing 7-10% a year in Japan, 10-14% in South-East Asia and 15-20% in the Middle East for organised and direct-to-consumer players; in Japan the direct-to-consumer share rose from 25% to 31% in five years and Owndays is the third-largest such chain with 287 stores against 500+ each for the top two (AR FY26).

blocks.callout: **So what:** the market grows ~13-14% a year in the company's own numbers, so Lenskart's 30% India growth comes mostly from taking share from unorganised opticians and from creating first-time buyers through free eye tests. That is a good sign (share gains have a long runway at 4-6% share) and a warning (growth depends on Lenskart keeping its cost and service edge as it moves into smaller towns).

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** the structural tailwind (more people needing glasses, more of them buying from organised chains) clearly reaches Lenskart: it is the largest organised player and is adding ~600 stores a year. The question is not demand but price: how much of this the share price already discounts (see valuation).

sections.title: India: revenue +30%, stores +26% a year, and margins still rising (15.4% after rent in Q1FY27)

blocks.p: India revenue rose from ₹4,061 cr in FY25 to ₹5,260 cr in FY26 (+29.5%) and ₹1,531 cr in Q1FY27 (+30.7%). Growth comes from three places: same-store sales (SSSG 20.8% in FY26, 24.2% in Q4FY26, 18.3% in Q1FY27), new stores (542 net in FY26, 116 in Q1FY27, two-thirds in Tier 2+ towns) and price/mix (India ASP ₹1,856 in Q1FY27, +6.4%). Units grew 22.8% in Q1FY27; eye tests 42.7%. Same-pin-code growth (SPSG, 24.3%) running ~6 points above SSSG is the company's evidence that new stores add demand rather than cannibalise.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** India is the engine and it is accelerating in stores but slowing in same-store growth (24.2% in Q4FY26, 18.3% in Q1FY27). sections.title: International: profitable at last, 10.6% margin after rent in Q1FY27, with few new stores

blocks.p: International revenue rose from ₹2,639 cr (FY25) to ₹3,606 cr (FY26, +36.7%, with Meller added and rupee weakness) and ₹1,203 cr in Q1FY27 (+38%; ~29% in constant currency). Only 61 net new stores were added in FY26 and 16 in Q1FY27: growth is same-store and online. Japan (Owndays) grew mainly through same stores with better unit economics; Singapore, Thailand and the UAE are growing online; the Middle East had 41 stores at Mar-2026; Meller (Spanish sunglasses brand, ~US$35 mn at acquisition) is tracking to ~US$70 mn and is now in 1,000+ Lenskart stores. Product margin is higher than India's (77.1% vs 64.2% in Q1FY27) because ASPs are ~3x (₹5,267 vs ₹1,856).

blocks.callout: **Our view:** management asks investors to read International on a trailing basis because Q1 carries the sunglasses season (units +58% in Q1FY27). We take 21.0% for FY27E before ESOP (FY26 19.3%; Q1FY27 21.9%) and add ~0.7-0.8 points a year. The risk is currency: International is ~41% of revenue and earns in yen, Singapore dollars and dirhams, so a stronger rupee would cut reported growth.

sections.title: Two margins tell the story: 21.7% before rent, 13.3% after rent in Q1FY27, against a ~25% long-term aim

blocks.p: Under Ind AS 116, store rent is not an operating expense: it becomes depreciation of a "right-of-use" asset plus interest on a lease liability. Lenskart's reported EBITDA (21.7% in Q1FY27) therefore excludes rent; its "EBITDA pre-IndAS 116" (13.3%) deducts it. The gap (~8 points) is the rent bill. Management's long-term aim of ~25% is on the after-rent basis, so even our FY29E (EBITDA {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}} before rent) implies only ~16-17% after rent.

bullets: **Product margin** (revenue less cost of goods) rose from 68.7% to 70.3% in Q1FY27 despite a weaker rupee against the renminbi: in-house frames and lenses (Bhiwadi, Thailand JV, Hyderabad from ~FY28) and premium mix.
**Employee cost** is the largest line (23% of FY26 revenue): optometrists and store staff. It rose with company stores (franchise buy-back) and new Tier 2+ stores are staffed before revenue ramps.
**Marketing** fell to 4.8% of India revenue in Q1FY27 (5.7% a year earlier); International stays ~9% as brands are built.
**Rent** fell to 5.8% of India revenue in Q4FY26 (6.5% a year earlier) as SSSG outran ~5% rent escalations; International 12.2%.

blocks.callout: **So what:** most of the margin gain since FY24 is operating leverage on a largely fixed store and head-office base. It continues only if same-store growth stays well above rent and wage inflation. With SSSG falling from 24% to 18% and openings shifting to smaller towns, we model ~1 point of segment margin a year, not the ~4 points of FY26.

sections.title: A real but narrow moat: scale in manufacturing and eye tests, not in brand pricing power

Unorganised opticians cannot match the reach; tests feed sales
3,459 stores; next-day delivery in 78 cities; stores double as service and pickup points
Hard to replicate quickly, but capital is the main barrier and well-funded rivals can build it

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** Lenskart has a genuine cost and reach advantage over unorganised opticians, which is where its share gains come from. It is a narrow moat in a fragmented market: it does not give pricing power, and returns depend on executing ~600 openings a year without hurting service. That is enough to justify a premium retail multiple; it is not a platform-style moat.

sections.title: Revenue up 2.3x in three years and EBITDA margin from 7% to 20%: Lenskart has crossed from losses to scale profits

blocks.p: Revenue went from ₹3,788 cr in FY23 (the first year with Owndays, which lifted revenue 152%) to ₹8,814 cr in FY26, 32.5% a year. EBITDA rose from ₹264 cr to ₹1,754 cr and the margin from 7.0% to 19.9% (after Ind AS 116, i.e. before rent; the company's own pre-IndAS 116 EBITDA, after rent, passed ₹1,000 cr in FY26, ~11% of revenue). Net profit after minorities went from a ₹64 cr loss in FY23 to ₹494 cr in FY26; FY25's ₹296 cr includes a ₹167 cr non-cash gain on the Owndays deferred consideration, so the underlying FY25 profit was ~₹130 cr. Three things drove the margin: product margin (revenue less materials) up from 64% to 71% as frames and lenses moved in-house; the switch from franchise (FoFo) to company stores (CoCo), which cut commissions from ₹733 cr to ₹181 cr while staff costs rose; and operating leverage on stores, marketing and head office.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the margin gain is real and mostly structural (manufacturing, franchise buy-backs, scale), not a one-year accident. But read the headline EBITDA carefully: it excludes rent. Rent (lease depreciation ₹704 cr and lease interest ₹163 cr in FY26) is the biggest cost of a store chain, and Lenskart's own pre-IndAS 116 margin was ~11% in FY26 and 13.3% in Q1FY27, against a long-term aim of ~25%.

bullets: **Growth yardstick:** Track annual volume growth of ~25% as 'the cleanest yardstick'; do not use any single quarter as the base expectation (FY26 volume +24.7%, Q1FY27 +25.7%).

**Stores:** Net new store additions in FY27 'at or around FY26 levels' (603 in FY26); 132 added in Q1FY27. India 'points past 10,000 stores' over time (6,100 unserved pin codes, ~3,000 densification).
**Margin:** Long-term steady-state EBITDA (pre-IndAS 116) margin ~25% (FY26 ~11%, Q1FY27 13.3%); near-term margins may vary with store phasing, marketing and long-term bets.

**Capex:** Hyderabad plant (~50 mn pairs a year) commissioning in ~18 months from May-2026, with a large part of the initial outlay in FY27; Q1FY27 capex ₹207 cr (stores ₹75 cr, plant ₹132 cr), funded from operating cash.
**International:** Measured store additions (16 in Q1FY27); margins to be judged on a trailing-twelve-month basis; Q1 benefits from the sunglasses season.

blocks.callout: **What we take from it:** a clean beat on margins, led by International (pre-IndAS margin 10.6% vs 4.5%) and product margin above 70%, with India growth still ~30%. The soft spots: India SSSG has come down from 24% to 18% in two quarters, and management is asking investors not to extrapolate any single quarter. Guidance is about volumes (~25%) and stores (~600), not profits.

sections.title: Stores pay for themselves; the IPO cash is still in the bank: ₹58 cr left over in FY26 after capex and rent

blocks.p: Over FY23-26 Lenskart generated ₹3,483 cr of operating cash and spent ₹2,106 cr on capex (Screener). Operating cash is flattered by Ind AS 116: rent is paid in the financing section. In FY26 operating cash of ₹1,670 cr paid for ₹829 cr of capex (603 net new stores, the Bhiwadi expansion and Hyderabad), ₹620 cr of lease principal and ₹163 cr of lease interest, leaving ₹58 cr (company: ₹34 cr "before M&A and IPO"). Acquisitions took another ₹421 cr (Meller, Dealskart and others), funded by pre-IPO cash. The ₹2,150 cr fresh issue (Nov-2025) was almost all unspent at Mar-2026 (₹177 cr used). Company-reported ROCE was 14.7% in FY26, 23.1% excluding idle IPO money, and 23.2% in Q1FY27.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** the store machine funds itself, and returns on the core are high (company: stores pay back in under a year). The open questions are the ₹4,104 cr of net cash (Jun-2026): Hyderabad (~₹1,500 cr estimated) will absorb a large part over FY27-28, and the IPO objects allow ₹683 cr for acquisitions and general purposes. Lenskart has been an active buyer (Owndays, Meller, Dealskart, GeoIQ, the Thailand JV); acquisitions at high prices are the main way returns could disappoint.

sections.title: Clean audit; three adjustments: proforma vs reported, rent outside EBITDA, and a one-off in FY25

bullets: **Two sets of numbers.** The letters quote "proforma" growth (Dealskart, GeoIQ and Meller consolidated in the base year); the audited accounts are "reported". From Q3FY26 the two are identical, but FY26 growth rates differ (Q1FY27 revenue +33.6% proforma, +43.3% reported). We use reported figures in the model and say when we quote proforma.

**EBITDA excludes rent.** Ind AS 116 moves rent into depreciation (right-of-use ₹704 cr) and interest (₹163 cr) and the cash into financing (lease principal ₹620 cr). Operating cash flow (₹1,670 cr) therefore overstates cash earnings; we treat lease principal as capex in the forecasts.

**FY25 one-off.** FY25 other income includes a ₹167 cr non-cash gain on the Owndays deferred consideration; FY26 includes ₹19 cr of liabilities written back and a call-option gain, and a ₹16 cr exceptional loss (investment impairment, IPO costs). Our forecasts carry none of these.
**Minorities.** ₹7.3 cr of FY26 profit and ~₹6-7 cr in Q1FY27 belong to minority partners; we use profit after minorities (LENSKART.patch.js) and load ~1.5 points onto the tax rate in forecasts.
**ESOP cost is small** (₹12.8 cr in FY26) because most options were granted before the IPO; grants at listed-market prices would raise it. We deduct ₹{{as.esop.0|num}}-{{as.esop.2|num}} cr a year.
**Goodwill** (₹2,198 cr) and brands (₹980 cr) from Owndays and Meller are tested for impairment yearly; no impairment of goodwill in FY26.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN-AMBER (we show AMBER).** S.R. Batliboi (EY) audits the accounts and we found nothing improper. The amber reflects the short like-for-like history, the proforma presentation in the letters and a headline EBITDA that excludes the largest store cost.

sections.title: Net cash of ₹3,881 cr before leases at Mar-2026 (₹4,104 cr at Jun-2026); ₹2,877 cr of lease liabilities

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 Lenskart held ₹4,100 cr of cash, deposits and liquid funds (₹1,544 cr cash and bank balances, ₹513 cr of investments, ₹2,013 cr of bank deposits in "other financial assets") against ₹220 cr of bank borrowings: net cash ₹3,881 cr on the company's definition. Lease liabilities were another ₹2,877 cr; Screener counts them as borrowings (₹3,097 cr), so its net debt figure below is not comparable with the company's. Goodwill and brands are large (₹2,198 cr and ₹980 cr, mostly Owndays and Meller). Inventory was 43 days of sales at Mar-2026 (59 days a year earlier); the company expects it to rise again as stock is rebuilt.

sections.title: Ownership: founders 17.5%; institutions doubled to 36% by Jun-2026 as pre-IPO investors sold

blocks.p: At Jun-2026 the founders (promoters) held 17.53%, foreign institutions 12.76%, Indian institutions 23.56% and others 45.73% (Screener's "public" includes the pre-IPO sovereign and venture holders). The six-month lock-up on pre-IPO shares ended on 8-May-2026 and the sovereign and venture investors began to sell: block deals of at least 8.15 cr shares at ₹473 that day (Alpha Wave, KKR's Birdseye View, TR Capital and others; buyers included Citi, BlackRock, Fidelity, HDFC MF and ICICI Pru MF), SoftBank 5.65 cr shares (3.25%) at ~₹509 on 3-Jun and a reported ADIA block of 4 cr shares at ₹490 on 11-Jun. Foreign institutions went from 4.3% (Mar-2026) to 12.8% and Indian institutions from 15.5% to 23.6% by Jun-2026. In the September quarter SoftBank sold another 4.5 cr shares at ₹642 (24-Aug; stake 9.86% → 7.28%), Alpha Wave sold ~2.95 cr shares at ₹630 (28-Aug, reported full exit) and an undisclosed holder sold ~3.5 cr shares at ₹688 (21-Sep); MSCI added the stock from 1-Sep.

But supply will keep meeting every rally until these funds are out.

sections.title: The street: 9 of 12 post-results notes are Buy; median target ₹707, all on EV/EBITDA after rent

blocks.p: Coverage began after the IPO quiet period (Jefferies, Macquarie, Emkay and Avendus in Nov-Dec 2025; Ambit published a Sell before listing) and widened in 2026 (Antique, Motilal Oswal, Elara, CLSA, BofA, J.P. Morgan, Nomura, ICICI Securities). After the Q1FY27 results (12-Aug-2026) 12 houses published dated targets: median ₹707 (+3% vs the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹685.05); including the older notes still standing, the median is ₹663. 9 are Buy or equivalent, Citi and HSBC are neutral and Ambit is the lone Sell (₹496). Every multiple we could confirm is EV/EBITDA on pre-IndAS (after-rent) EBITDA 1.5-2 years forward: Motilal Oswal 49x Sep-28E, Emkay 56x Jun-28E, Equirus 58x, Jefferies and Elara 50x FY28E; JM Financial (DCF, 53x implied) and ICICI Securities (DCF, ~48x India implied). Nobody uses P/E or EV/Sales as the main method; Bloomberg consensus P/E was 119x / 87x one/two-year forward (Motilal Oswal, 9-Sep-2026).

Bloomberg consensus (Motilal Oswal, 9-Sep-2026): post-IndAS EBITDA ₹2,726 cr / ₹3,460 cr and PAT ₹1,011 cr / ₹1,391 cr one/two years forward; EV/EBITDA 44.4x / 35.0x, P/E 119x / 87x at ₹692. 20 analysts on Bloomberg, 10 Buy (Business Today, 13-Aug-2026).

exhibit.title: Critiques we take seriously
head: Argument
rows: The headline EBITDA excludes rent. After rent (pre-IndAS) the margin was ~11% in FY26 and 13.3% in Q1FY27; the street's 48-58x multiples are applied to that smaller after-rent number.
India SSSG fell from 24.2% (Q4FY26) to 18.3% (Q1FY27); Equirus links part of it to negative publicity. Growth is shifting to new, smaller-town stores with lower revenue per store.
Ambit (Sell, ₹496): a capex-heavy, made-to-order model whose free cash flow lags its profit; Citi and HSBC (Neutral/Hold): the valuation already prices much of the growth.
Rupee weakness against the renminbi and yen raises the cost of imported frames and components; the product margin has held so far through in-house manufacturing.
Supply: pre-IPO funds have sold ~20% of the company since May-2026 and still hold large stakes.
Acquisitive: Owndays, Meller, Dealskart, GeoIQ and the Thailand JV in four years; ₹683 cr of IPO money is earmarked for acquisitions and general purposes.

sections.title: Valuation: 27x Sep-28E EBITDA gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}; the market pays 33.4x

blocks.p: The street uses EV/EBITDA on EBITDA after rent ("pre-IndAS 116"), 1.5-2 years forward, at 48-58x. We use the same method on the same date (Sep-28E: half FY28E, half FY29E) but on reported EBITDA before rent, with lease liabilities (₹2,877 cr at Mar-2026) counted as debt. The two are equivalent ways of treating rent; ours is the one on which the stock's own history and our model can be measured consistently. To compare, our target equals **41.2x** Sep-28E EBITDA after rent (₹2,255 cr, our estimate) on the street's basis. The "At our EBITDA" column applies each broker's multiple to our after-rent EBITDA.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a strong business at 33.4x Sep-28E EBITDA; SELL on valuation, not on quality

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's largest organised eyewear company, growing ~30% with ~600 new stores a year, a ~70% product margin from its own factories, an International business that has just become properly profitable (10.6% margin after rent in Q1FY27), ₹4,104 cr of net cash and a long runway (4-6% share of a market that is itself being created). The quality is not in question.

**What you are paying:** ₹685.05 is 135.7x our FY27E and 98.7x FY28E EPS, and 33.4x Sep-28E EBITDA before rent (≈50.1x after rent on the street's basis). Since listing the stock has traded at a median 30.6x forward EBITDA; retail multiples have fallen ~12% over the same months. The street (median ₹707) pays 48-58x after-rent EBITDA, a premium the stock's own short history and the sector's de-rating do not support under our rule.

**This is a valuation call, not a business call.** Our EPS is in the middle of the street (FY28E ₹6.94 vs ₹5.6-8.4); the gap is the multiple: the street's 48-58x after-rent EBITDA vs our ≈41.2x, which comes from Lenskart's own 30.6x median since listing and the retail sector's de-rating.
